title: Retirement shift exposes super funds’ technology challenge
full_text:
Australia’s super funds will need greater investment in technology and payment systems as the shift towards retirement income places new demands on infrastructure built to accumulate savings, according to J.P. Morgan.
Its 2026 Future of Superannuation report identified legacy systems, cybersecurity risks and funding constraints as barriers to funds becoming the central point for members’ retirement needs.
Drawing on 11 interviews with senior executives, including leaders at funds managing more than $1 trillion for over 10 million members, the report found operational infrastructure is being stretched by the industry’s growth.
AustralianSuper head of retirement Jacki Ellis said delivering retirement income brought expectations shaped by members’ experiences with their banks.
“You become a payment provider when you’re a retirement provider,” Ellis said. “Most Australians’ expectations around payments are set through their interactions with banks, and superannuation funds are a long way from that seamless experience today.”
The report argued that better retirement products and advice would need to be supported by reliable payments, secure systems and platforms capable of delivering more personalised services.
State Super chief executive, John Livanas, highlighted the consequences of payment disruptions for members who relied on regular pension income.
“We pay 68,000 pensions every fortnight – that’s around $3 billion a year,” Livanas said. “If those payments are delayed by even a few days, it becomes a serious issue. Imagine being a pensioner, having saved all your working life to create a pension which you rely on for your day to day living. Imagine then, that one Monday there’s not enough money in your bank account to go buy groceries.
“That’s why we invest a huge amount of time and effort to ensure payments are made on time.”
Cybersecurity added another challenge, with the report pointing to the April 2025 attack on Australian super funds, which used previously leaked usernames and passwords to target pension drawdown accounts. Attackers attempted to redirect or initiate lump sum withdrawals after gaining access.
Vanguard Australia chief of personal investor, Renae Smith, said the transition towards managing retirement income at scale was increasing funds’ exposure to fraud and scams, with deepfakes and more sophisticated cyber threats making member protection increasingly important.
Australian Retirement Trust principal, retirement solutions Brnic Van Wyk said protecting information and maintaining payments were increasingly central to fund operations.
“When it comes to the super industry’s technology base and architecture, we all need to be focused on cybersecurity, our ability to protect information, our ability to pay people. Increasingly, our boardroom is becoming a technology business.”
Van Wyk also suggested funds could pursue more strategic partnerships to improve retirement payments, including closer integration with banks.
“Superannuation funds need to be able to get money to members as seamlessly as a bank does. There should be a way where we can integrate with the bank so that if a member asks us for money, we put it straight into their bank account instantaneously.”
The report cited fund expenditure data showing 60 APRA-regulated super funds spent $900 million on IT services in 2024–25, although outsourcing arrangements and spending recorded under other categories complicated comparisons.
By comparison, Commonwealth Bank increased its annual investment spending by $300 million to $2.3 billion in 2024–25 and hired 2,000 IT engineers, according to the report.
J.P. Morgan identified a tension between the investment required to improve services and continuing pressure on funds to keep fees low. It also noted that legacy platform upgrades or replacements could involve lengthy periods offline.
Cbus chief strategy officer Bernie Dean said banks had benefited from substantially more time to develop their systems.
“Banks have had sometimes four and five times the number of decades to mature their systems and liquidity management and their experience of consumer behaviour than what we have.”
Funds were already investing in upgrades, with HESTA general manager, retirement Shannon O’Shea saying its new administration platform was supporting real-time member updates, greater data transparency and improved service integration.
Ellis said further investment would need to extend beyond retirement products and advice.
“I think there’ll need to be quite an investment and innovation in registry systems and platforms, not just product suites and the advice and guidance of platforms over the next decade to be able to set ourselves up for the system we need to become for the future.”
